def: To make someone feel intimidated or apprehensive.
ex: Do not let the sheer size of the technical codebase daunt you during onboarding.
nat: The difficult mountain trail did not daunt the experienced hikers.

mis.bad: The big challenge daunted to him.
mis.good: The big challenge daunted him.
mis.why: "Daunt" is transitive; do not use "to".

def: Seeming difficult to deal with in anticipation; intimidating.
ex: Migrating forty legacy microservices to the cloud in three weeks felt daunting to everyone.
nat: Learning a new language from scratch can seem daunting at first.

mis.bad: I felt very daunting about the project.
mis.good: I felt very daunted by the project / The project felt daunting.
mis.why: Use "daunting" for the task and "daunted" for the feeling.

def: To blind someone temporarily with very bright light, or impress greatly.
ex: The bright oncoming high-beam headlights dazzle drivers on dark country roads at night.
nat: Her solo violin performance managed to dazzle the international classical critics.

mis.bad: The presentation dazzled to everyone.
mis.good: The presentation dazzled everyone.
mis.why: "Dazzle" takes a direct object without "to".

def: Extremely bright, impressive, beautiful, or skillful.
ex: She gave a dazzling keynote presentation on the future of generative artificial intelligence models.
nat: The tropical island offers dazzling white sand beaches and clear blue waters.

mis.bad: He did a very dazzled presentation.
mis.good: He gave a dazzling presentation.
mis.why: Use "dazzling" to describe something that impresses; "dazzled" describes someone impressed.

def: Causing or able to cause death; extremely lethal.
ex: Certain venomous spiders found in tropical regions can deliver a deadly neurotoxic bite.
nat: The police uncovered a deadly weapon hidden inside the suspect's vehicle.

mis.bad: The snake has a dead poison.
mis.good: The snake has a deadly venom / poison.
mis.why: Use "deadly" as an adjective meaning lethal, not "dead".

def: An agreement entered into by two or more parties for mutual benefit.
ex: The two technology companies finalized a multi-million dollar software licensing deal yesterday afternoon.
nat: Finding a good deal on flights requires booking several weeks in advance.

mis.bad: We made a deal with them to selling the house.
mis.good: We made a deal with them to sell the house.
mis.why: Use "make a deal to + base verb", not "to -ing".

def: Scattered fragments, typically of something wrecked or destroyed.
ex: Emergency rescue crews cleared fallen building debris from the streets after the hurricane.
nat: Space debris orbiting the Earth poses an increasing threat to commercial satellites.

mis.bad: There were many debries on the floor.
mis.good: There was a lot of debris on the floor.
mis.why: "Debris" is uncountable and the "s" is silent (/dəˈbriː/); never write "debries".

def: Characterized by or reflecting a state of moral or cultural decline, or luxuriously indulgent.
ex: We enjoyed a rich and decadent chocolate dessert at the French restaurant tonight.
nat: Historians debate whether late Roman society was truly as decadent as chronicled.

mis.bad: The building was decadent (meaning dilapidated).
mis.good: The building was dilapidated / run-down.
mis.why: In English, "decadent" often means luxurious or self-indulgent; for physically crumbling structures use "dilapidated" or "run-down".

def: To cause someone to believe something that is not true, typically for personal gain.
ex: Scammers often use fake bank logos to deceive unsuspecting customers into sharing passwords.
nat: Do not deceive yourself into believing that skipping tests will save time.

mis.bad: He deceived to his best friend.
mis.good: He deceived his best friend.
mis.why: "Deceive" is transitive and takes no "to".

def: The action of deceiving someone; a trick or scheme intended to mislead.
ex: The corporate auditor exposed a complex web of financial deception within the firm.
nat: She could not forgive his deliberate deception regarding where the money went.

mis.bad: He made a big decepção to his parents.
mis.good: He was a big disappointment to his parents.
mis.why: False cognate: English "deception" means trickery or fraud; Portuguese "decepção" is "disappointment".

def: Giving an appearance or impression different from the true one; misleading.
ex: Appearances can be deceptive, so always inspect the apartment thoroughly in person.
nat: The advertisement made deceptive claims about the health benefits of the herbal supplement.

mis.bad: The contract has a deceptive clause (meaning disappointing).
mis.good: The contract has a deceptive clause (meaning tricky) / disappointing clause.
mis.why: Remember: "deceptive" means misleading or fraudulent, not disappointing.

def: To convert code into normal language, or succeed in understanding something obscure.
ex: It took the cryptographer three days to decipher the intercepted encrypted radio message.
nat: I could barely decipher the doctor's handwritten medical notes on the prescription.

mis.bad: He deciphered out the puzzle.
mis.good: He deciphered the puzzle / figured out the puzzle.
mis.why: Do not say "decipher out"; "decipher" is used alone.

def: Settling an issue; producing a definite result; or having the ability to decide firmly.
ex: A good executive must remain calm and decisive during unexpected corporate public crises.
nat: The late goal in the final minutes proved decisive for the championship match.

mis.bad: He is not very decidive.
mis.good: He is not very decisive.
mis.why: Spelled with "s": "decisive", not "decidive".

def: A formal or explicit statement or announcement.
ex: The prime minister issued an official declaration regarding the emergency state of health.
nat: You must complete a customs declaration form before entering the foreign country.

mis.bad: Make a declare at the customs desk.
mis.good: Make a declaration at the customs desk.
mis.why: Use the noun "declaration", not the verb "declare".

def: To devote time, effort, or oneself to a particular task or purpose.
ex: She decided to dedicate thirty minutes every morning to studying professional English vocabulary.
nat: The author dedicated his latest historical novel to his supportive grandmother.

mis.bad: He dedicated his time for learn English.
mis.good: He dedicated his time to learning English.
mis.why: Use "dedicate [time] to + -ing", not "for + base verb".

def: Devoted to a task or purpose; having single-minded loyalty; or assigned to a specific function.
ex: Our engineering department has a dedicated team handling cloud infrastructure and production security.
nat: She is a dedicated teacher who stays late to help struggling students.

mis.bad: We have a server dedicated for backups.
mis.good: We have a server dedicated to backups.
mis.why: Use "dedicated to [a purpose]", not "for".

def: The quality of being dedicated or committed to a task or purpose.
ex: Her dedication to improving patient healthcare outcomes earned her a national medical award.
nat: The book features a touching dedication page honoring the author's late parents.

mis.bad: He has much dedicate to his career.
mis.good: He shows great dedication to his career.
mis.why: Use the noun "dedication", not the verb "dedicate".

def: To subtract or take away an amount or part from a total.
ex: Employers deduct federal income tax and health insurance premiums directly from paychecks.
nat: You can deduct legitimate business travel expenses on your annual tax return.

mis.bad: They deducted of my salary.
mis.good: They deducted the amount from my salary.
mis.why: Use "deduct [amount] from [total]", not "deduct of".

def: The action of deducting or subtracting something, or the inference of particular instances.
ex: Tax deductions can significantly lower the total amount of money you owe annually.
nat: Through logical deduction, the detective identified the only person with access to the safe.

mis.bad: I made a logic deduct.
mis.good: I made a logical deduction.
mis.why: Use "logical deduction", not "logic deduct".

def: To regard or consider in a specified way.
ex: The committee will deem the proposal acceptable only if security standards are met.
nat: The safety inspector deemed the ancient stone stairway unsafe for public pedestrian use.

mis.bad: The manager deemed him like unfit.
mis.good: The manager deemed him unfit.
mis.why: "Deem" is followed directly by an adjective or noun without "like" or "as".

def: A preselected option adopted automatically, or failure to fulfill a legal/financial obligation.
ex: The application restores your settings to default if the configuration file becomes corrupted.
nat: Rising mortgage interest rates led to a sudden increase in loan defaults.

mis.bad: The phone came with standard defauts.
mis.good: The phone came with default settings.
mis.why: Spelled "default" in English, with an "l".

def: To win a victory over someone in a battle, game, or contest.
ex: Our basketball team managed to defeat our main cross-town rivals by two points.
nat: Do not let a single temporary failure defeat your long-term professional aspirations.

mis.bad: They defeated from the other team.
mis.good: They were defeated by the other team / They lost to the other team.
mis.why: In the active voice: "A defeated B". To say you lost, use passive "we were defeated by" or "we lost to".

def: A shortcoming, imperfection, or lack in someone or something.
ex: Quality control detected a critical manufacturing defect in the lithium car battery pack.
nat: Engineers patched a minor defect in the payment authentication protocol this morning.

mis.bad: The software has many defects (meaning bugs).
mis.good: The software has several bugs / defects.
mis.why: In software, "bug" or "defect" is standard; stress is on the first syllable (/ˈdiːfekt/) for the noun.

def: Imperfect or faulty; not working correctly.
ex: Customers can return defective electronics within thirty days for a full cash refund.
nat: The vehicle recall was triggered by defective passenger airbag sensors across multiple models.

mis.bad: The keyboard came defectuous.
mis.good: The keyboard came defective.
mis.why: The English adjective is "defective" or "faulty", not "defectuous".

def: The action of defending from or resisting attack; or the defendant's case in court.
ex: A multi-factor authentication layer provides a strong defense against automated credential stuffing attacks.
nat: The defense attorney presented convincing alibi evidence to the jury this afternoon.

mis.bad: They played a good defesy.
mis.good: They played good defense.
mis.why: Spelled "defense" in American English and "defence" in British English.

def: Used or intended to defend or protect; very anxious to challenge or avoid criticism.
ex: He became immediately defensive when his manager gently pointed out three coding errors.
nat: The team adopted a defensive strategy to protect their narrow lead until halftime.

mis.bad: She reacted in a defensory way.
mis.good: She reacted in a defensive way / got defensive.
mis.why: Use the adjective "defensive", not "defensory".

def: Open resistance; bold disobedience against authority or rules.
ex: In open defiance of company policy, several employees leaked internal documents to reporters.
nat: Her calm defiance inspired thousands of citizens to join the peaceful public protest.

mis.bad: He acted with much defy.
mis.good: He acted with great defiance.
mis.why: Use the noun "defiance", not the verb "defy".

def: Showing open resistance, bold disobedience, or defiance.
ex: The teenager remained defiant even after the school principal threatened a one-week suspension.
nat: She held a defiant attitude throughout the entire hostile cross-examination by prosecutors.

mis.bad: He gave a defianted response.
mis.good: He gave a defiant response.
mis.why: The English adjective is "defiant", not "defianted".

def: A lack or shortage of something, especially of a nutrient or essential element.
ex: A severe vitamin D deficiency can weaken bones and affect daily immune system function.
nat: The financial audit revealed serious internal control deficiencies in the accounting department.

mis.bad: He has an auditory deficiency (meaning hearing loss).
mis.good: He has hearing impairment / hearing loss.
mis.why: In English, bodily sensory issues are termed "impairment" or "loss"; "deficiency" refers to nutrient lack or system shortcomings.

def: Not having enough of a specified quality or ingredient; insufficient.
ex: A diet deficient in dietary fiber can lead to chronic digestive and health problems.
nat: The architectural safety plan was found deficient in several key emergency evacuation areas.

mis.bad: The food is deficient of iron.
mis.good: The food is deficient in iron.
mis.why: Use "deficient in [a nutrient/quality]", not "of".

def: To state or describe exactly the nature, scope, or meaning of something.
ex: Clear team leaders always define individual project roles before starting any collaborative sprint.
nat: How would you define personal career success at this stage of your life?

mis.bad: We need to define about the roadmap.
mis.good: We need to define the roadmap.
mis.why: "Define" is transitive; do not use "about".

def: Done or reached decisively and with authority; providing a final solution.
ex: The medical board published a definitive guide to managing diabetes through healthy lifestyle.
nat: We are still waiting for a definitive answer from the executive hiring committee.

mis.bad: He gave a definitely answer.
mis.good: He gave a definitive answer.
mis.why: Do not confuse the adjective "definitive" with the adverb "definitely".

def: To let air or gas out of something, or reduce someone's confidence.
ex: Remember to deflate the inflatable camping mattress before packing it into your backpack.
nat: The harsh negative critique from the reviewer completely deflated the young author's spirits.

mis.bad: The tire deflated out completely.
mis.good: The tire deflated completely.
mis.why: Avoid adding "out"; "deflate" already means lose air.

def: To cause something to change direction; turn aside from a straight course.
ex: Politicians frequently attempt to deflect difficult interview questions by changing the discussion topic.
nat: The goalie managed to deflect the speeding soccer ball with his fingertips.

mis.bad: He deflected of the question.
mis.good: He deflected the question.
mis.why: "Deflect" is transitive; do not add "of".

def: To break down chemically, deteriorate physically, or treat someone with contempt.
ex: Certain biodegradable plastics degrade naturally when exposed to moist soil and sunlight conditions.
nat: No manager should ever degrade or humiliate an employee in front of colleagues.

mis.bad: The battery degrades down after two years.
mis.good: The battery degrades after two years.
mis.why: Do not add "down"; "degrade" already expresses decline.

def: The condition or process of deteriorating or being degraded.
ex: Deforestation causes severe soil degradation, which reduces agricultural yields across affected farming regions.
nat: She felt a deep sense of degradation after being falsely accused of theft.

mis.bad: We must prevent the degrade of the river.
mis.good: We must prevent the degradation of the river.
mis.why: Use the noun "degradation", not the verb "degrade".

def: To deprive of human qualities, personality, or dignity.
ex: Treating warehouse workers like automated robots tends to dehumanize labor and damage morale.
nat: War propaganda often attempts to dehumanize enemy soldiers to justify brutal violence.

mis.bad: The system deshumanizes people.
mis.good: The system dehumanizes people.
mis.why: Spelled with "de-", not Portuguese "des-": "dehumanize".

def: The assignment of authority to another person, or a body of delegates.
ex: Effective task delegation allows senior managers to focus on high-impact strategic growth initiatives.
nat: An official trade delegation from Brazil met with business leaders in Frankfurt today.

mis.bad: He has trouble with delegate of tasks.
mis.good: He has trouble with delegation of tasks / task delegation.
mis.why: Use the noun "delegation", not the verb "delegate".

def: Done consciously and intentionally; fully considered; unhurried.
ex: The security audit revealed that the data deletion was a deliberate inside attack.
nat: She spoke in a slow, deliberate tone to ensure everyone understood every point.

mis.bad: It was not a deliberate thing (if accidental).
mis.good: It was an accident / It was not deliberate.
mis.why: Use "deliberate" directly as a predicate adjective.

def: Very fine in texture or structure; easily broken; or requiring sensitive handling.
ex: Negotiating salary increases is a delicate topic that requires polite, professional diplomacy.
nat: The antique glass vase is extremely delicate, so handle it with great care.

mis.bad: This is a very delicade situation.
mis.good: This is a very delicate situation.
mis.why: Spelled "delicate" with a "t", not "delicade".

def: Great pleasure; something that gives great pleasure or satisfaction.
ex: It was an absolute delight to meet your family at the annual barbecue.
nat: To the delight of shareholders, the company declared a record quarterly cash dividend.

mis.bad: I have a big delight for reading.
mis.good: Reading is a great delight to me / I take great delight in reading.
mis.why: The idiom is "take delight in [something]".

def: The action of delivering letters, packages, or ordered goods; manner of speaking.
ex: The courier scheduled the parcel delivery between two and four this Wednesday afternoon.
nat: Her confident vocal delivery made the technical presentation engaging from beginning to end.

mis.bad: I am waiting for the deliver.
mis.good: I am waiting for the delivery.
mis.why: Use the noun "delivery" for the package/shipment; "deliver" is the verb.

def: An insistent and peremptory request, or the desire of consumers for goods.
ex: Consumer demand for electric vehicles has surged dramatically across European cities this year.
nat: The union submitted a formal list of wage and safety demands to management.

mis.bad: There is much demand of engineers.
mis.good: There is high demand for engineers.
mis.why: Use "demand for [something]", not "demand of".

def: Requiring much skill, effort, or attention; making high claims on one's patience.
ex: Working as a software architect on live banking systems is an extremely demanding job.
nat: She has a very demanding boss who expects email replies even on weekends.

mis.bad: My job is very demandant.
mis.good: My job is very demanding.
mis.why: The English adjective is "demanding", not "demandant".

def: To cause a severe loss in the dignity of and respect for someone.
ex: I refuse to demean myself by engaging in petty office gossip and backstabbing.
nat: Insulting remarks demean the entire profession and discourage young people from joining.

mis.bad: He demeaned to his assistant.
mis.good: He demeaned his assistant.
mis.why: "Demean" is transitive; do not use "to".

def: Outward behavior or bearing towards others.
ex: His calm, professional demeanor during the production crisis reassured all team members immediately.
nat: The suspect maintained a quiet, reserved demeanor throughout the entire police interrogation.

mis.bad: She had a polite comportment.
mis.good: She had a polite demeanor.
mis.why: In English, outward bearing is usually "demeanor" or "manner"; "comportment" is archaic.

def: To pull or knock down a building; or completely refute an argument.
ex: The city decided to demolish the abandoned warehouse to make room for a public park.
nat: Her thorough evidence easily demolished the prosecutor's flawed theory in front of the jury.

mis.bad: They demolished down the house.
mis.good: They demolished the house / tore down the house.
mis.why: Do not say "demolish down"; use "demolish" or "tear down".

def: The action or process of demolishing or being demolished.
ex: Safety barricades were installed around the site before scheduled demolition work began yesterday.
nat: The sports team handed their rivals a complete demolition, winning six to zero.

mis.bad: We watched the demolish of the tower.
mis.good: We watched the demolition of the tower.
mis.why: Use the noun "demolition", not the verb "demolish".

def: The action of declaring something to be untrue; refusal to acknowledge an unpleasant reality.
ex: Living in denial about mounting credit card debt will only make the problem worse.
nat: The government issued a flat denial of any involvement in the foreign cyberattack.

mis.bad: He is in denegation of the truth.
mis.good: He is in denial about the truth.
mis.why: The English noun is "denial", not "denegation".

def: Closely compacted in substance; having parts crowded together.
ex: We drove cautiously through dense morning fog along the dangerous winding coastal highway.
nat: The academic textbook was so dense with mathematical jargon that few students finished it.

mis.bad: The forest was very densy.
mis.good: The forest was very dense.
mis.why: The adjective is "dense", not "densy".

def: The degree of compactness of a substance; quantity of people or things in an area.
ex: The urban planner studied the population density of central Tokyo compared to London.
nat: Lead has a much higher physical density than aluminum or lightweight carbon fiber.

mis.bad: The city has a big denseness.
mis.good: The city has high population density.
mis.why: Use "density" rather than "denseness".

def: To publicly declare to be wrong or evil; inform against someone.
ex: World leaders gathered at the summit to denounce the unprovoked military aggression strongly.
nat: Former members stepped forward to denounce the cult's abusive internal practices to authorities.

mis.bad: He denounced the theft to the police (meaning reported).
mis.good: He reported the theft to the police.
mis.why: False cognate: "denounce" means publicly condemn; to notify police about a crime use "report".

def: To leave, typically in order to start a journey; deviate from an accepted course.
ex: Our international flight is scheduled to depart from gate forty-two at eight tonight.
nat: The new corporate policy departs significantly from our company's traditional working methods.

mis.bad: The train departs to Rio.
mis.good: The train departs for Rio / leaves for Rio.
mis.why: Use "depart for [a destination]", not "to".

def: Contingent on or determined by; relying on someone or something else for support.
ex: Children remain financially dependent on their parents while completing full-time university degree programs.
nat: Our company revenue is heavily dependent on three major global enterprise clients.

mis.bad: I am dependent of coffee.
mis.good: I am dependent on coffee.
mis.why: Always use "dependent on", never "dependent of".

def: Trustworthy and reliable; capable of being relied on consistently.
ex: She is the most dependable engineer on our team whenever emergencies strike production.
nat: My old Japanese car may be noisy, but it is remarkably dependable every winter.

mis.bad: He is a very dependent person (meaning reliable).
mis.good: He is a very dependable person.
mis.why: Do not confuse "dependent" (needing support) with "dependable" (reliable).

def: To feel or express strong disapproval of something.
ex: Educational leaders deplore the continuous budget cuts hitting public primary schools nationwide.
nat: We deplore all forms of workplace discrimination and harassment within our global organization.

mis.bad: We deplore about the tragedy.
mis.good: We deplore the tragedy.
mis.why: "Deplore" is transitive; do not use "about".

def: To make someone feel utterly dispirited or dejected; reduce economic activity.
ex: Gloomy rainy weather for ten consecutive days can easily depress anyone's daily mood.
nat: High interest rates continue to depress consumer borrowing and retail spending across markets.

mis.bad: The sad news depressed to me.
mis.good: The sad news depressed me.
mis.why: "Depress" is transitive; do not use "to".

def: In a state of general unhappiness or despondency; suffering from clinical depression.
ex: He felt depressed after receiving the third job rejection email of the week.
nat: The economic crisis left many manufacturing towns financially depressed for several decades.

mis.bad: I am feeling depressing today.
mis.good: I am feeling depressed today.
mis.why: Use "-ed" for the person experiencing the feeling: "depressed", not "depressing".

def: Causing or resulting in a feeling of miserable or dispirited unhappiness.
ex: Walking through the abandoned, windowless office building on a gray morning was depressing.
nat: It is depressing to see how much plastic waste washes up on beaches.

mis.bad: The movie had a very depressed ending.
mis.good: The movie had a very depressing ending.
mis.why: Use "-ing" for the thing that causes the emotion: "depressing ending".

def: The damaging lack of material benefits considered to be basic necessities in society.
ex: Chronic sleep deprivation impairs cognitive memory consolidation and weakens the human immune system.
nat: Children raised in severe economic deprivation face substantial obstacles to academic success.

mis.bad: He suffered with food deprival.
mis.good: He suffered food deprivation.
mis.why: The English noun is "deprivation", not "deprival".

def: To deny a person or place the possession or use of something essential.
ex: Working eighty hours a week will inevitably deprive you of quality family time.
nat: The cruel prison guards attempted to deprive the inmates of access to water.

mis.bad: The law deprives him from his rights.
mis.good: The law deprives him of his rights.
mis.why: Always use "deprive [someone] of [something]", not "from".

def: The distance from the top or surface to the bottom of something.
ex: The swimming pool has a maximum depth of three meters at the deep end.
nat: Her latest historical novel explores emotional themes with extraordinary psychological depth and nuance.

mis.bad: We discussed the topic in deep.
mis.good: We discussed the topic in depth.
mis.why: The idiom is "in depth" (noun), not "in deep".

def: In a very poor condition as a result of disuse and neglect.
ex: The city converted the derelict railway terminal into a vibrant covered community food market.
nat: Police discovered several stolen vehicles parked behind the derelict textile factory at midnight.

mis.bad: The house was completely derelicted.
mis.good: The house was completely derelict.
mis.why: The adjective form is "derelict", not "derelicted".

def: To move or fall downward; or pass by inheritance.
ex: Passengers must remain seated with seatbelts fastened as the airplane begins to descend.
nat: A heavy mountain mist descended rapidly over the quiet village as dusk fell.

mis.bad: The airplane descended down quickly.
mis.good: The airplane descended quickly.
mis.why: Avoid saying "descend down"; "descend" already means go down.

def: A person, plant, or animal that is descended from a particular ancestor.
ex: She is a direct descendant of the famous nineteenth-century abolitionist and orator.
nat: Modern domestic chickens are actually evolutionary descendants of fierce prehistoric theropod dinosaurs.

mis.bad: He is an ascendee of the royal family.
mis.good: He is a descendant of the royal family.
mis.why: Use "descendant" for offspring; "ancestor" is the forefather.

def: An action of moving downward, dropping, or falling; or a person's origin/lineage.
ex: The plane began its final descent into Frankfurt airport twenty minutes before landing.
nat: She is of Brazilian descent and speaks fluent Portuguese with her grandparents.

mis.bad: He made a quick descend of the hill.
mis.good: He made a quick descent of the hill.
mis.why: Use the noun "descent", not the verb "descend".

def: To give an account in words of someone or something, including all characteristics.
ex: Can you describe the user interface bug you encountered while submitting the payment?
nat: The witness accurately described the suspect's clothing and vehicle to the police detective.

mis.bad: Please describe about what happened.
mis.good: Please describe what happened.
mis.why: "Describe" is transitive; do not use "about".

def: A spoken or written representation or account of a person, object, or event.
ex: Please read the detailed job description carefully before submitting your formal job application.
nat: The police officer wrote down a precise description of the stolen luxury vehicle.

mis.bad: Write a describe of your project.
mis.good: Write a description of your project.
mis.why: Use the noun "description", not the verb "describe".

def: Serving or seeking to describe something in an objective or vivid manner.
ex: Her travel blog contains rich descriptive passages about local food and cultural traditions.
nat: Linguists prefer descriptive grammar that observes natural speech over rigid prescriptive rules.

mis.bad: The report was very descriptor.
mis.good: The report was very descriptive.
mis.why: The English adjective is "descriptive", not "descriptor" (which is a noun).

def: To appoint someone to a specified position; officially assign a specified status.
ex: The board decided to designate Maria as the official project manager for deployment.
nat: The city designated this central street as a pedestrian-only zone on weekends.

mis.bad: They designated him like the team leader.
mis.good: They designated him as the team leader.
mis.why: Use "designate [someone] as [role]", not "like".

def: The action of choosing someone or specifying something for a purpose, or an official title.
ex: Her official job designation was changed from senior analyst to director of operations.
nat: The national park received an international biosphere reserve designation from UNESCO last year.

mis.bad: What is your office design (meaning title)?
mis.good: What is your official designation / job title?
mis.why: In English, "designation" refers to an official title or classification; "design" is styling/layout.

def: The complete loss or absence of hope.
ex: Do not give in to despair when your early startup experiments fail to gain traction.
nat: A deep sense of despair gripped the city following the devastating earthquake report.

mis.bad: He was in deep desperate (noun).
mis.good: He was in deep despair.
mis.why: Use the noun "despair", not the adjective "desperate", after "in deep".

def: Feeling, showing, or involving a hopeless sense that a situation is impossible to deal with.
ex: The stranded mountain climbers made a desperate bid to reach shelter before nightfall.
nat: Hospitals in rural provinces are in desperate need of certified nurses and doctors.

mis.bad: I am very desperate with this noise.
mis.good: This noise is driving me crazy / I feel desperate.
mis.why: In Portuguese, "estar desesperado" is often used colloquially for being stressed or annoyed; in English "desperate" implies real extremity or hopelessness.

def: To feel contempt or a deep repugnance for someone or something.
ex: I despise dishonesty and political manipulation in professional work environments above everything else.
nat: She despised the cold, dark northern winter months and longed to move south.

mis.bad: He despised of his rival.
mis.good: He despised his rival.
mis.why: "Despise" is transitive; do not insert "of".

def: To persuade someone not to take a particular course of action.
ex: Our senior engineer tried to dissuade management from choosing an unproven database framework.
nat: Nothing could dissuade her from pursuing her dream of studying overseas.

mis.bad: He dissuaded me to buy the car.
mis.good: He dissuaded me from buying the car.
mis.why: Use "dissuade [someone] from + -ing", not "to + base verb".

def: In low spirits from loss of hope or courage; dejected.
ex: He grew despondent after months of sending job applications without receiving a single interview.
nat: Fans looked despondent as the referee blew the final whistle on their defeat.

mis.bad: She was despondent with the bad news.
mis.good: She was despondent about the bad news.
mis.why: Use "despondent about/over", not "with".

def: To end the existence of something by damaging or attacking it.
ex: A single undetected security breach can destroy consumer trust built over many years.
nat: High waves and strong winds destroyed several coastal wooden piers along the boardwalk.

mis.bad: The fire destroyed down the house.
mis.good: The fire destroyed the house.
mis.why: Do not add "down"; "destroy" already expresses complete demolition.

def: The action or process of causing so much damage to something that it no longer exists.
ex: The hurricane caused widespread physical destruction across the low-lying coastal island towns.
nat: We must prevent the unnecessary destruction of ancient tropical rainforest ecosystems for mining.

mis.bad: The war left a big destroy.
mis.good: The war caused massive destruction.
mis.why: Use the noun "destruction", not the verb "destroy".

def: Causing great and irreparable harm or damage.
ex: Excessive personal criticism in team retrospectives can become destructive to collaboration and morale.
nat: Termites are remarkably destructive insects that can compromise a wooden building's structural foundation.

mis.bad: He has a very destructful attitude.
mis.good: He has a very destructive attitude.
mis.why: The English adjective is "destructive", not "destructful".

def: To disengage and remove something from a larger unit or whole.
ex: You can detach the tablet screen from the keyboard dock for reading comfortably.
nat: The astronaut had to detach the tether before returning safely into the airlock.

mis.bad: Please detach the paper of the notebook.
mis.good: Please detach the sheet from the notebook.
mis.why: Use "detach from [something]", not "of".

def: Separate or disconnected, or aloof and objective in emotional attitude.
ex: A good judge must remain emotionally detached when evaluating evidence in high-profile criminal trials.
nat: They bought a charming single-family detached house in the leafy residential suburb.

mis.bad: He lived in a house detached (meaning apart).
mis.good: He lived in a detached house.
mis.why: Put the adjective "detached" before the noun: "detached house".

def: To keep someone from proceeding; hold in custody.
ex: Customs border agents may detain suspicious travelers for additional baggage and passport inspection.
nat: Heavy traffic on the highway detained our delivery van for over forty minutes.

mis.bad: The police detained to the suspect.
mis.good: The police detained the suspect.
mis.why: "Detain" is transitive; do not use "to".

def: An individual feature, fact, or item; a small part of something.
ex: The software architect explained every technical detail of the caching layer during standup.
nat: She has an extraordinary eye for detail when reviewing contract terms and conditions.

mis.bad: Let me explain this in details.
mis.good: Let me explain this in detail.
mis.why: The standard English expression is "in detail" (singular), not "in details".

def: Having many details or facts; thorough and comprehensive.
ex: The senior developer wrote a detailed onboarding guide for new team hires yesterday.
nat: Please send me a detailed estimate of material and labor costs before Friday.

mis.bad: He gave an explanation very detail.
mis.good: He gave a very detailed explanation.
mis.why: Use the adjective "detailed", not the noun "detail".

def: The action or process of identifying the presence of something concealed.
ex: Early detection of cancerous tumors dramatically increases a patient's chances of full recovery.
nat: Modern intrusion detection systems alert cloud administrators to anomalous network traffic patterns instantly.

mis.bad: The virus escaped to the detection.
mis.good: The virus escaped detection.
mis.why: Say "escape detection", not "escaped to the detection".

def: The process of becoming progressively worse in quality or condition over time.
ex: Engineers noticed rapid structural deterioration in the concrete support pillars under the highway.
nat: A sudden deterioration in diplomatic relations prompted embassy staff to leave the country.

mis.bad: The house suffered a big deteriorate.
mis.good: The house suffered severe deterioration.
mis.why: Use the noun "deterioration", not the verb "deteriorate".

def: To dislike intensely; feel great hatred or repugnance for.
ex: I detest waking up before sunrise on cold, dark winter Monday mornings.
nat: She detests office politics and prefers to focus entirely on deep engineering work.

mis.bad: I detest of waiting in line.
mis.good: I detest waiting in line.
mis.why: "Detest" is transitive; do not use "of".

def: Tending to cause harm or damage; unfavorable.
ex: Lack of sleep is deeply detrimental to your long-term memory retention and physical health.
nat: Frequent context switching has a detrimental effect on software engineering team focus.

mis.bad: Smoking is very detrimentous to health.
mis.good: Smoking is detrimental to health.
mis.why: The English adjective is "detrimental", not "detrimentous".

def: To destroy or ruin something completely, or cause someone overwhelming grief.
ex: The category five hurricane threatened to devastate coastal fishing villages along the shore.
nat: Hearing the unexpected news of the company closure will completely devastate the workers.

mis.bad: The fire devastated down the forest.
mis.good: The fire devastated the forest.
mis.why: Do not add "down"; "devastate" already means destroy completely.

def: Highly destructive or damaging; causing extreme shock, grief, or distress.
ex: The sudden earthquake delivered a devastating blow to the nation's transportation infrastructure.
nat: She received the devastating news that her research funding had been cancelled completely.

mis.bad: The tsunami was very devastator.
mis.good: The tsunami was devastating.
mis.why: The English adjective is "devastating", not "devastator".

def: Great destruction or damage across an area or community.
ex: Reporters documented scenes of utter devastation in the wake of the severe floodwaters.
nat: The sudden factory shutdown brought economic devastation to the entire small industrial town.

mis.bad: The war left a big devastate.
mis.good: The war left immense devastation.
mis.why: Use the noun "devastation", not the verb "devastate".

def: To grow or cause to grow and become more mature, advanced, or elaborate.
ex: Our startup plans to develop an open-source tool for managing Kubernetes container clusters.
nat: Some individuals develop mild lactose intolerance as they enter adult middle age.

mis.bad: We need to develop about our strategy.
mis.good: We need to develop our strategy.
mis.why: "Develop" is transitive; do not use "about".

def: The process of developing or being developed, or an event constituting a new stage.
ex: Investing in employee professional development reduces annual corporate staff turnover rates significantly.
nat: Recent diplomatic developments in the region offer real hope for lasting bilateral peace.

mis.bad: Check the develop of the project.
mis.good: Check the development of the project.
mis.why: Use the noun "development", not the verb "develop".

def: Entirely lacking or free from something specified.
ex: His formal speech was surprisingly dry and devoid of any genuine emotional warmth.
nat: The arid desert landscape appeared almost completely devoid of plant and animal life.

mis.bad: The essay was devoid with good arguments.
mis.good: The essay was devoid of good arguments.
mis.why: Always use "devoid of", never "with".

def: Love, loyalty, or enthusiasm for a person, activity, or spiritual cause.
ex: Her selfless devotion to teaching underprivileged children inspired the whole community deeply.
nat: He practiced his violin scales with religious devotion for three hours every single morning.

mis.bad: He has a big devotion by music.
mis.good: He has great devotion to music.
mis.why: Use "devotion to [a cause/person]", not "by".

def: To eat food hungrily or quickly, or read something eagerly and rapidly.
ex: Starving after the long mountain hike, the teenagers devoured the entire pepperoni pizza.
nat: She devoured the entire mystery trilogy in just two days during summer vacation.

mis.bad: He devoured down the meal.
mis.good: He devoured the meal.
mis.why: Do not add "down"; "devour" already implies consuming greedily.

def: Concerned with the diagnosis of illness or other problems; serving to identify.
ex: The automobile mechanic ran a computerized diagnostic test to identify the engine rattling noise.
nat: The clinic offers comprehensive diagnostic imaging services, including magnetic resonance tomography scans.

mis.bad: The doctor gave me a diagnostic (noun).
mis.good: The doctor gave me a diagnosis.
mis.why: Distinguish the noun "diagnosis" (result) from the adjective "diagnostic" (identifying tool/test).

def: To lay down authoritatively; prescribe; or say aloud for another to write.
ex: Market supply and consumer demand dictate the fluctuating prices of seasonal agricultural commodities.
nat: The doctor will dictate the medical summary notes into the automated transcription software.

mis.bad: The boss dictated to us what to do.
mis.good: The boss dictated to us what to do / dictated what we should do.
mis.why: Use "dictate [rules/terms]" directly.

def: A ruler with total power over a country, typically one who obtained it by force.
ex: The ruthless military dictator suppressed all independent press and banned political opposition parties.
nat: History shows that even the most powerful dictators eventually lose their tyrannical grip.

mis.bad: The country was ruled by a dictador.
mis.good: The country was ruled by a dictator.
mis.why: Spelled with "t": "dictator", not "dictador".

def: A difference between amounts, values, or rates of something; distinguishing feature.
ex: The significant salary differential between remote workers and onsite employees sparked heated debate.
nat: Our company's main competitive differential is exceptional twenty-four hour customer support responsiveness.

mis.bad: Our competitive differencial is speed.
mis.good: Our competitive differential is speed.
mis.why: Spelled with "t": "differential", not "differencial".

def: To recognize or identify what makes someone or something different.
ex: Can you differentiate between authentic customer reviews and automated bot-generated praise comments?
nat: Our innovative mobile user experience will differentiate our fintech app from traditional competitors.

mis.bad: He cannot differentiate of the twins.
mis.good: He cannot differentiate between the twins.
mis.why: Use "differentiate between A and B", not "of".

def: To spread over a wide area or among a large number of people.
ex: A skilled mediator knows how to diffuse tension before heated workplace conflicts explode.
nat: The essential oil burner will diffuse the calming lavender scent throughout the office.

mis.bad: He tried to defuse/diffuse the bomb (spelling).
mis.good: He diffused the light / He defused the tension.
mis.why: Note: "diffuse" means spread out; "defuse" specifically means deactivate a bomb or crisis, though "diffuse tension" is also used metaphorically.

def: To break down food in the stomach, or assimilate and understand new information.
ex: Give yourself time to digest the complex technical documentation before beginning code implementation.
nat: Eating a heavy dinner right before bedtime makes it much harder to digest properly.

mis.bad: I need to digest out this news.
mis.good: I need to digest this news.
mis.why: Do not add "out"; "digest" is used alone.

def: The process of breaking down food by mechanical and enzymatic action in the stomach.
ex: Drinking warm water with fresh lemon after meals can aid your daily digestion.
nat: Poor digestion is often linked to eating meals too quickly under severe stress.

mis.bad: He has problems with his digest.
mis.good: He has digestive problems / problems with his digestion.
mis.why: Use the noun "digestion", not "digest".

def: The state or quality of being worthy of honor or respect; self-respect.
ex: Every human being deserves to be treated with fundamental dignity and mutual respect.
nat: Despite losing the heated election, the mayor conceded defeat with extraordinary personal dignity.

mis.bad: He lost his dignitary (meaning dignity).
mis.good: He lost his dignity.
mis.why: A "dignitary" is a person of high rank; "dignity" is the quality of honor.

def: To leave the main subject temporarily in speech or writing.
ex: Let me digress for a moment to explain why this database schema choice matters.
nat: Speakers who constantly digress often lose the attention of their corporate audience quickly.

mis.bad: Do not digress of the main point.
mis.good: Do not digress from the main point.
mis.why: Use "digress from [a topic]", not "of".

def: In a state of disrepair or ruin as a result of age or neglect.
ex: They bought a dilapidated historic farmhouse in Tuscany and spent years renovating it beautifully.
nat: The city condemned the dilapidated commercial dock after several rotten wooden planks collapsed.

mis.bad: The car was very dilapidating.
mis.good: The car was dilapidated.
mis.why: Use the past participial adjective "dilapidated", not "-ing".

def: To make or become wider, larger, or more open.
ex: Your pupils naturally dilate in dark rooms to allow more ambient light to enter.
nat: The eye doctor used medicated drops to dilate the patient's pupils for examination.

mis.bad: The cold weather dilates the veins.
mis.good: Cold weather constricts the veins (widen is dilate).
mis.why: Remember: "dilate" means widen/expand; "constrict" means shrink/narrow.

def: Careful and persistent work or effort; thorough attentiveness.
ex: Due diligence is absolutely essential before acquiring or merging with an overseas technology startup.
nat: Her academic diligence throughout the rigorous semester resulted in straight top honors grades.

mis.bad: They made the due diligency.
mis.good: They conducted due diligence.
mis.why: The English noun is "diligence" (ends in "-ce"), not "diligency".

def: To make a liquid thinner or weaker by adding water or another solvent.
ex: You should dilute concentrated bleach with plenty of cold water before cleaning bathroom tiles.
nat: Issuing too many company shares will dilute the equity value of existing shareholders.

mis.bad: Dilute down the juice with water.
mis.good: Dilute the juice with water.
mis.why: Omit "down"; "dilute" already expresses thinning a solution.

def: A measurable extent of some kind, such as length, breadth, depth, or height.
ex: Please verify the exact dimensions of the dining table before ordering it online.
nat: Working remotely full-time adds an entirely new dimension to team leadership and communication.

mis.bad: What are the sizes dimensions of the bed?
mis.good: What are the dimensions of the bed?
mis.why: Say "dimensions" or "measurements", not both together.

def: Extremely or unusually small; tiny.
ex: Despite her diminutive physical stature, she possessed an immensely powerful and commanding vocal presence.
nat: The chef served a diminutive chocolate truffle dusted with cocoa powder after dinner.

mis.bad: He has a diminute car.
mis.good: He has a diminutive car.
mis.why: The English word is "diminutive", not "diminute".

def: In a way that addresses situations tactfully and without offending others.
ex: The project lead diplomatically explained to the client that the deadline was unrealistic.
nat: She handled the awkward team disagreement diplomatically, keeping both sides calm and cooperative.

mis.bad: He answered in a diplomatic way.
mis.good: He responded diplomatically / in a diplomatic way.
mis.why: Both "diplomatically" and "in a diplomatic way" are correct.

def: Extremely serious, urgent, or dreadful.
ex: The hurricane left the impoverished coastal community in dire need of clean drinking water.
nat: Scientists warned that continuing current carbon pollution rates will have dire global ecological consequences.

mis.bad: They were in a very dirous situation.
mis.good: They were in a dire situation.
mis.why: The English adjective is "dire", not "dirous".

def: A book or computer file listing names, addresses, phone numbers, or electronic folders.
ex: Make sure you run the terminal command inside the correct project root directory.
nat: The hotel lobby provides an interactive touch-screen directory of all local city attractions.

mis.bad: Save the file in the pasta.
mis.good: Save the file in the folder / directory.
mis.why: False cognate: Portuguese "pasta" in computing is "folder" or "directory".

def: A physical or mental condition that limits a person's movements, senses, or activities.
ex: Living with a permanent physical disability requires tremendous daily resilience and accessible public infrastructure.
nat: She receives monthly disability benefits following a severe back injury at the factory.

mis.bad: He has an intellectual deficient.
mis.good: He has an intellectual disability.
mis.why: Use "person with an intellectual disability" rather than calling someone a "deficient".

def: Having a physical or mental condition that limits their movements, senses, or activities; deactivated.
ex: Accessible parking spaces near the supermarket entrance are reserved exclusively for disabled drivers.
nat: The system administrator temporarily disabled the compromised user account to stop the breach.

mis.bad: He is a deficiente.
mis.good: He has a disability / He is disabled.
mis.why: In modern English, refer to "a person with a disability" or "a disabled person".

def: To have or express a different opinion; or fail to correspond.
ex: I respectfully disagree with your conclusion that automated testing replaces human user research.
nat: Spicy food often disagrees with my sensitive stomach when traveling in foreign countries.

mis.bad: I am disagree with you.
mis.good: I disagree with you.
mis.why: Never say "I am disagree"; "disagree" is a normal active verb ("I disagree").

def: Lack of consensus or approval; an argument or dispute.
ex: A minor disagreement over software styling standards should never escalate into personal conflict.
nat: The two business partners decided to separate peacefully due to persistent strategic disagreements.

mis.bad: They had a disaccord about the money.
mis.good: They had a disagreement about the money.
mis.why: The English noun is "disagreement", not "disaccord".

def: To cease to be visible; pass out of sight in a sudden manner.
ex: The early morning ocean mist will disappear completely as soon as the sun rises.
nat: My car keys seem to disappear mysteriously every time I am in a hurry.

mis.bad: He disappeared with the money (meaning stole).
mis.good: He ran off with the money / disappeared with the money.
mis.why: Note spelling: single "s", double "p": "disappear".

def: An instance of someone or something ceasing to be visible or no longer existing.
ex: Police launched an extensive investigation into the sudden disappearance of the valuable art piece.
nat: The rapid disappearance of ancient coral reefs alarms marine biologists around the globe.

mis.bad: The disappear of the document was strange.
mis.good: The disappearance of the document was strange.
mis.why: Use the noun "disappearance", not the verb "disappear".

def: A sudden event that causes great damage or serious loss of life.
ex: The unexpected hurricane was the worst natural disaster to hit the province in decades.
nat: Failing to test database backups regularly is a recipe for complete corporate disaster.

mis.bad: The presentation was a complete desastre.
mis.good: The presentation was a complete disaster.
mis.why: Spelled with "i": "disaster", not "desastre".

def: Causing great damage; highly unsuccessful or catastrophic.
ex: The botched software deployment had disastrous financial consequences for the entire online shopping platform.
nat: A disastrous crop harvest left thousands of local farming families in acute poverty.

mis.bad: It was a desastrous mistake.
mis.good: It was a disastrous mistake.
mis.why: Spelled "disastrous" (without the "e" from disaster).

def: To break up and stop functioning as a cohesive organized group.
ex: After ten years of successful worldwide touring, the iconic rock band decided to disband.
nat: The international peacekeeping coalition disbanded after completing its scheduled humanitarian mission successfully.

mis.bad: They desbanded the team.
mis.good: They disbanded the team.
mis.why: Spelled with "dis-", not Portuguese "des-": "disband".

def: To get rid of someone or something as no longer useful or desirable.
ex: Please discard all expired refrigerated food items into the designated outdoor compost bin.
nat: You can safely discard these printed draft notes once the digital document updates.

mis.bad: Discard out the bad apples.
mis.good: Discard the bad apples / Throw out the bad apples.
mis.why: Do not say "discard out"; use "discard" alone or "throw out".

def: To perceive or recognize something, often with difficulty using senses or intellect.
ex: It was difficult to discern the faint outline of the distant lighthouse through fog.
nat: A seasoned interviewer can quickly discern genuine passion from rehearsed corporate interview answers.

mis.bad: I cannot discern of the truth.
mis.good: I cannot discern the truth.
mis.why: "Discern" is transitive; do not use "of".

def: Able to be discerned; perceptible to the human senses or intellect.
ex: There was no discernible difference in page load speeds between the two server frameworks.
nat: Her voice showed a barely discernible tremor when announcing her unexpected company resignation.

mis.bad: There was no discernive change.
mis.good: There was no discernible change.
mis.why: The English adjective is "discernible" (or "discernable"), not "discernive".

def: To allow someone to leave hospital, release a liquid/gas, or fire a weapon.
ex: Doctors agreed to discharge the recovering surgery patient from the hospital this Thursday morning.
nat: The industrial factory was fined heavily for discharging toxic chemical waste into the river.

mis.bad: He was discharged of the hospital.
mis.good: He was discharged from the hospital.
mis.why: Use "discharge from [hospital/military]", not "of".

def: A personal follower of a teacher, leader, or philosopher during their life.
ex: The renowned martial arts master trained a small group of highly disciplined disciples.
nat: Modern agile software coaches often view themselves as disciples of lean manufacturing principles.

mis.bad: He is a discipular of that philosophy.
mis.good: He is a disciple of that philosophy.
mis.why: The English noun is "disciple", not "discipular".

def: A state of physical or mental unease or mild distress.
ex: You may experience minor muscle discomfort for a day or two after weightlifting.
nat: His invasive personal questions caused noticeable discomfort among everyone sitting around the table.

mis.bad: I felt a big disconfort in my back.
mis.good: I felt a lot of discomfort in my back.
mis.why: Spelled with "m": "discomfort", not "disconfort".

def: To break the connection of or between two entities; detach.
ex: Always disconnect the electronic power cable before opening the desktop computer case for repairs.
nat: It is healthy to disconnect completely from work emails during your scheduled annual vacation.

mis.bad: Disconnect the cable of the wall.
mis.good: Disconnect the cable from the wall.
mis.why: Use "disconnect from [something]", not "of".

def: Lack of contentment; dissatisfaction with one's circumstances or with authority.
ex: Mounting employee discontent over sudden mandatory office return policies sparked a petition drive.
nat: Low wages and high inflation fueled widespread public discontent throughout the capital city.

mis.bad: There is much descontent in the company.
mis.good: There is much discontent in the company.
mis.why: Spelled with "dis-", not Portuguese "des-": "discontent".

def: Disagreement between people; lack of harmony between musical notes or groups.
ex: Unresolved compensation inequalities created bitter personal discord among the original software startup founders.
nat: A harsh musical discord broke the peaceful melody of the orchestral string quartet.

mis.bad: He created much discording in the team.
mis.good: He sowed a lot of discord in the team.
mis.why: Use the noun "discord", not "discording".

def: To cause someone to lose confidence or enthusiasm; dissuade someone from doing something.
ex: Do not let initial grammar mistakes discourage you from practicing spoken English with native speakers.
nat: High luxury tariffs are designed to discourage consumers from buying imported fuel-heavy vehicles.

mis.bad: The rain discouraged us to go out.
mis.good: The rain discouraged us from going out.
mis.why: Always use "discourage [someone] from + -ing", not "to + base verb".

def: The action or process of discovering or being discovered, or something found.
ex: The research laboratory made a breakthrough discovery that could revolutionize electric battery storage capacities.
nat: Finding that quiet neighborhood Italian bakery was the sweetest discovery of our Rome trip.

mis.bad: They made a big discover yesterday.
mis.good: They made a big discovery yesterday.
mis.why: Use the noun "discovery" for the finding; "discover" is the verb.

pt: discreto (que guarda segredo / não chama atenção)
def: Careful and circumspect in one's speech or actions, especially to avoid offense or scandal.
ex: The private investigator promised to remain completely discreet throughout the entire sensitive family inquiry.
nat: She gave him a discreet nod across the conference table to begin speaking.

mis.bad: He is very discrete about secrets (spelling error).
mis.good: He is very discreet about secrets.
mis.why: Distinguish "discreet" (cautious/secretive) from "discrete" (separate/distinct).

def: Individually separate and distinct; not continuous.
ex: Computer science mathematics represents data using discrete binary numbers rather than continuous analog values.
nat: The engineering project was broken down into five discrete development phases for management.

mis.bad: The steps were very discreet (meaning distinct).
mis.good: The steps were discrete.
mis.why: Spelled "discrete" (-ete) when meaning mathematically or logically distinct; "discreet" (-eet) means tactful/secretive.

def: The quality of behaving in a way to avoid offense; freedom to decide.
ex: The executive assistant handled all confidential executive salary files with utmost personal discretion.
nat: Managers have the discretion to grant remote work days during harsh winter weather.

mis.bad: Use your own discreet (noun).
mis.good: Use your own discretion.
mis.why: Use the noun "discretion", not the adjective "discreet".

def: The feeling that someone or something is unworthy of one's consideration or respect.
ex: The senior architect looked with open disdain at the sloppy, completely untested code snippet.
nat: She treated superficial status symbols with profound disdain, prioritizing authentic human connections instead.

mis.bad: He spoke with desdém about his rivals.
mis.good: He spoke with disdain about his rivals.
mis.why: The English noun is "disdain", not "desdém".

def: Loss of reputation or respect as the result of a dishonorable action; a cause of shame.
ex: The corrupt executive resigned in total disgrace after being convicted of corporate embezzlement charges.
nat: Leaving elderly patients without warm blankets in winter is an absolute administrative disgrace.

mis.bad: The scandal was a big desgrace.
mis.good: The scandal was a huge disgrace.
mis.why: False cognate note: in Portuguese "desgraça" often means misfortune/tragedy; in English "disgrace" means shame, dishonor, or scandal.

def: To give a new appearance to someone or something to hide their identity.
ex: The undercover security agent wore a tourist outfit to disguise his real investigative purpose.
nat: She tried unsuccessfully to disguise the bitter disappointment trembling in her vocal tone.

mis.bad: He disguised of a doctor.
mis.good: He disguised himself as a doctor / dressed up as a doctor.
mis.why: Use "disguise oneself as [someone]", not "of".

def: To disappoint someone by breaking their belief in an illusion or false ideal.
ex: Working inside government bureaucracy quickly disillusioned the idealistic young political science college graduate.
nat: I hate to disillusion you, but the deadline will not be extended again.

mis.bad: He was desilusioned with his job.
mis.good: He was disillusioned with his job.
mis.why: Spelled "disillusioned" with "dis-", double "l", and double "s".
